decisions.decision: Claiming ALREADY asks about the parent Requirement's state, for exactly one status, and that is the decisive measurement. internal/application/service.go:1130-1142 -- V2-065's guard -- reads the parent inside Claim's transaction through requirementAwaitsHumanInput (declared at internal/application/human_input.go:683-695) and refuses with ErrAwaitingHumanInput (human_input.go:288) when the status is needs-input, and internal/api/api.go:1253-1259 maps that error to 409 conflict. So this task adds NO read, NO port, NO transaction and NO new place where the parent is consulted: it widens a question the code already asks from a one-member set to the complement of the set that admits work, at the same line, in the same transaction, with the same shape. Measured: the parent read costs nothing new because it is the same u.Requirement call the needs-input guard already performs, and the same helper's second caller, Service.Renew (service.go:284-288), is deliberately NOT touched -- see d6. That is why this task is a two-line guard plus a fixture migration, and not a redesign.
decisions.rationale: Framing the task as 'add a question' would have produced a second parent read, a second definition of 'the parent's state' and a second refusal error, and would have put the new guard in a different place from the existing one -- which is how the needs-input refusal would silently change its precedence. Framing it as 'widen the question already asked' fixes the position (immediately after the existing guard), fixes the error class (a state conflict returning 409, not a permit denial), and makes the whole risk surface the fixture migration rather than the mechanism. The mechanism is measured to be one switch statement.

decisions.decision: The set of statuses that admit work is {ready, active, waiting, recovering} -- FOUR of the eleven -- and it is DERIVED rather than chosen. The derivation is one product sentence plus one existing domain branch. docs/product/definition.md:111 is the requirement: '3. 利用可能なworkerが、実行可能なRequirementを排他的にclaimする。' -- an available worker claims an EXECUTABLE Requirement, which is the product asking claiming to ask. docs/architecture/domain-model.md:266 says what a claim PRODUCES: '`active` | 1つ以上のIncrementが進行中'. So a Requirement admits a claim if and only if it may legally be active once the claim lands, and the domain already answers that question in exactly one place: internal/domain/model.go:485-489, whose allowed(...) call at :486 admits RequirementStart from exactly RequirementReady, RequirementRecovering and RequirementWaiting. Add RequirementActive, which is already there and needs no transition, and the set is closed at four. The product agrees cell by cell: domain-model.md:265 lists `active` among ready's targets, :267 among waiting's, :270 among recovering's, and :266 is active itself. Nothing is written out a second time: the four statuses are declared ONCE, in internal/application/claimable.go, and the test proves that declaration equal to {s : DecideRequirement(s, RequirementStart) succeeds} union {active} over the complete status axis.
decisions.rationale: Choosing the set by taste is how non_goals item 2 gets violated, and every plausible taste-based answer was measured and rejected. {ready, active} alone is the intuitive answer and it is WRONG: domain-model.md:267 and :270 both list `active` as a transition target, and internal/domain/model.go:486 admits the start command from both, so refusing a claim from waiting or recovering would refuse a claim the Requirement's state actually admits -- exactly non_goals item 2. Measured, that wrong answer is also invisible in the test suite: not one existing fixture claims from waiting or recovering (see d4), so {ready, active} would have passed every test in the repository while being wrong. The wider set costs zero fixtures and is the only one derivable from the product. Deriving from the domain's own branch rather than from domain-model.md's transition table is deliberate and is defended in d3.

decisions.decision: The authority for the set is the domain's RequirementStart branch, NOT domain-model.md's '主な遷移先' column, and the disagreement between them is measured, recorded and NOT repaired. The table is WIDER than the branch by exactly TWO cells: domain-model.md:268 lists `active` among needs-input's targets and :271 lists `active` among evaluating's, while model.go:486 admits the start command from neither. The tie is broken by the product itself in the needs-input case, and that is what settles the evaluating case too: docs/product/definition.md:143 defines pause claim as '新しい仕事のclaimを止める' and V2-065 built exactly that for needs-input -- internal/application/service.go:1139-1142 refuses new claims while a question is open, and internal/application/human_input_test.go:534-587's biconditional asserts that the refusal and the displayed ScopeNewClaimsForThisRequirement agree in both directions. So the product demonstrably does NOT treat 'the table lists active as a target' as 'a claim is admitted': needs-input is a counterexample already shipped and already asserted. evaluating is refused for the same reason and for a second measured one: with evaluating outside model.go:486's admitted set, a claim from evaluating would put an Increment 進行中 under a Requirement that the domain forbids from becoming active, so V2-084's parent transition would do nothing and the aggregate would contradict domain-model.md:266. The two-cell gap is logged as a named finding for the tech_lead and asserted nowhere.
decisions.rationale: This is the sharpest judgement in the task and getting it wrong in either direction is a defect. Widening the set to follow the table would admit claims from needs-input and break a shipped, product-cited refusal -- and would require editing internal/application/human_input.go, which is why that file is prohibited rather than merely unused. Narrowing internal/domain to match the table would move a state machine this task has no licence to move and would drag internal/domain/** and its edge-count guards into a task whose whole point is that the domain already answers the question. Recording rather than asserting follows the reason internal/application/framing_test.go:562-564 already gives: asserting a defect pins it in place and turns its repair into a failure in a file the repairing task may not own.

decisions.decision: The fixture migration, measured by EXECUTION rather than by reading, at 9bf0d8c. The guard was implemented in a throwaway copy of this worktree and the whole suite run. Result: 45 top-level tests fail in 17 test files across 4 packages without an emulator, and TestFirestoreApplicationAtomicityConflictAndControl (internal/store/firestore/store_test.go:179) fails as a 46th in an 18th file and a 5th package when scripts/firestore-emulator.sh is started for real -- measured, not inferred. The refusals number 64: 60 distinct (test-or-subtest, Increment) pairs in internal/application, internal/reconciler and internal/runner, 2 in internal/api and 2 in internal/store/firestore, over 62 distinct Increments. And the single most useful number in this packet: the offending parent status was `captured` in 60 of 60 cases where the error text was observable, and in ZERO cases anything else -- no framing, no paused, no evaluating, no cancelled, and no missing or empty parent link (`grep -o 'parentstatus=\[[a-z-]*\]' | sort | uniq -c` returned exactly `60 parentstatus=[captured]`). The migration is therefore ONE shape repeated 62 times, not 62 different problems.
decisions.rationale: The Work Order this task inherits guessed at the blast radius by counting files -- V2-084's A6 predicted 18 test files calling Claim, which is exactly right as a file count (measured: 18 files, 46 call sites) and useless as a migration estimate, because a file that calls Claim is not the same thing as a fixture that breaks. Running the guard produced the real number and, more importantly, the real SHAPE: every affected fixture is in the same state for the same reason, so one migration table with one status column is enough to make weakening visible. Uniformity is what makes the acceptance criteria in the Work Order checkable rather than aspirational.

decisions.decision: A missing or unlinked parent REFUSES, and the choice is made on design grounds because measurement proves it free. Both variants were built and run: permissive (an Increment whose RequirementID is empty, or whose parent is not in the store, is admitted) and strict (both refuse). The failing sets are BYTE-IDENTICAL -- 45 tests, 60 refusals, and `comm` over the two sorted failure lists returns nothing on either side -- so no fixture in the repository claims an Increment with a missing or empty parent, and the choice is unobservable in the current suite. Strict is correct: 'the Requirement it belongs to is not in a state that admits work' is satisfied by a Requirement that cannot be read at all, and definition.md:111's 実行可能 cannot be established for a record that does not exist. This is ALSO the reason the new predicate is a second helper rather than a widening of requirementAwaitsHumanInput: that helper answers a narrower question ('is it in needs-input'), for which unknown correctly means no, and it returns false for an empty id (human_input.go:685-687) and for a missing record (:691-693). The two questions have OPPOSITE correct answers on the unknown case, so sharing one helper would force one of them to be wrong.
decisions.rationale: An implementer who reached for the existing helper and widened its switch would have shipped a guard that admits every claim whose parent link is empty -- and would then have had a hole nothing in the suite could see, because no fixture exercises it. Measuring both variants turned a stylistic preference into a decided fact with a stated reason, and the opposite-polarity argument is what makes 'two helpers' a structural conclusion rather than duplication. Both must therefore be asserted explicitly, since no existing test reaches either case.

decisions.decision: Service.Renew is NOT touched, and internal/application/human_input.go and human_input_test.go are PROHIBITED. Renew's guard at internal/application/service.go:284-288 keeps asking only the needs-input question. The reason is measured and is written in the tree already: service.go:1131-1138 records that the needs-input refusal is closed on the ISSUING side on purpose, because no domain transition can revoke or release an active lease early (domain.ExpireLease refuses while at is before ExpiresAt), so a refusal can only ever mean 'no NEW claim'. definition.md:143 says the same thing from the product side -- pause claim stops 新しい仕事のclaim, and '実行中の仕事が進める「定義済みの境界」はcheckpointであり' -- so a lease already held is carried to a checkpoint, not killed. Widening Renew would kill work already in flight the moment a parent moved to paused or evaluating, which is a harder stop than the product describes anywhere. Prohibiting human_input.go and human_input_test.go converts that into a build constraint: the V2-065 refusal, its error, its position and its biconditional test cannot be edited, so if the new guard masks or reorders the needs-input refusal the ONLY remedy is to fix the new guard.
decisions.rationale: The tempting move is 'the parent's state should gate both, they are the same question' -- and it is wrong for a reason that is written down in the code being read. Making the prohibition carry the argument is worth more than a sentence in a scope note: internal/application/human_input_test.go:534's TestTheDisplayedStoppedScopeAndTheClaimRefusalAgree is a biconditional whose refusal arm t.Fatalf's on 'Claim failed for an unrelated reason', so it fails loudly the instant the new refusal leaks into a needs-input fixture or the instant the new guard is ordered ahead of the old one. That test is the best tripwire in the repository for this specific mistake, and it is worth more untouched than editable.

decisions.decision: The refusal is a state CONFLICT, not a control denial, and it is ordered before the permit. A new sentinel application.ErrRequirementNotClaimable is declared in a new file internal/application/claimable.go and wrapped with the increment id exactly as the needs-input refusal is wrapped at service.go:1142. It is classified at internal/api/api.go:1253-1259 by adding one disjunct to the EXISTING 409-conflict branch that already carries ErrAwaitingHumanInput, because the reason written in that branch's comment applies verbatim: nothing the caller can rewrite makes the claim issuable while the parent is in that state. Measured, this classification is mandatory rather than cosmetic: with the guard in place and api.go unedited, internal/api/api_test.go:1176 recorded `claims:acquire: status 500` with body `{"error":"internal_error"}` -- an unclassified refusal, which additionally fires V2-088's operator record for an unclassified error. The guard sits immediately after the needs-input guard at service.go:1139-1142 and therefore BEFORE the canonical-target resolution and the domain.Permit evaluation, so when a Requirement admits no work AND a stop is in force the caller sees ErrRequirementNotClaimable. That precedence is a decision and must be asserted in both directions rather than left to the reader.
decisions.rationale: The three wrong answers here are all attractive. Reusing ErrAwaitingHumanInput would make a paused or cancelled Requirement report that it is waiting for a human answer, which is a lie the owner console would repeat. Returning domain.ErrControlDenied would put a state fact in the control plane's vocabulary and would make it indistinguishable from a stop, corrupting the stop matrix's meaning. Leaving it unclassified was measured and produces a 500, which is the worst of the three because it reads as a control-plane fault. Ordering before the permit preserves the existing needs-input precedence byte for byte -- the alternative would have required moving a shipped guard -- and asserting the precedence in both directions is what stops it from drifting the next time a branch is inserted.

decisions.decision: The set is declared once and read twice, and the second read is derived from source so the closure survives a new status. internal/application/claimable.go declares requirementStatusAdmitsClaim as one switch over four domain constants. A new test file internal/application/claimable_test.go then reads it twice: (i) against the COMPLETE RequirementStatus axis derived by parsing internal/domain/model.go with go/ast -- the idiom internal/application/allocation_test.go already uses, which declares allocDomainDir = "../domain" at allocation_test.go:624 and parses that directory at :309, and which internal/application/framing_test.go:159-211 uses for a source-level issuer count -- so a twelfth RequirementStatus added later enters the table unclassified and fails it; and (ii) against the domain's own answer, asserting for every status on that axis that requirementStatusAdmitsClaim(s) is true if and only if domain.DecideRequirement(Requirement{ID, Status: s, Version: v}, RequirementCommand{Kind: RequirementStart, ...}) returns a nil error OR s == RequirementActive. internal/domain/** is PROHIBITED, so the four-status list exists in exactly one file and the domain's branch exists in exactly one file, and any drift between them is a red test rather than a silent widening.
decisions.rationale: The failure mode this design most has to prevent is an implementer adding `captured` to the switch, which would make all 62 fixtures green with zero fixture edits. A hand-written table of eleven expected answers is not enough on its own: an implementer editing the switch would edit the table in the same breath, and both edits look local and reasonable. The equivalence assertion is different in kind, because making `captured` admitted requires ALSO widening internal/domain/model.go:486 -- which is prohibited -- so the wrong answer becomes unreachable rather than merely discouraged. Deriving the axis from source rather than writing eleven constants closes the other end: a status added later cannot quietly default to admitted or to refused.

decisions.decision: The eleven-cell table is the acceptance for both non_goals items 2 and 3, and it is exhaustive over the status axis at TWO altitudes. Altitude one, pure and cheap, in claimable_test.go: for every status on the go/ast-derived axis, the predicate's answer, plus the domain equivalence of d8, plus the two unknown-parent cells of d5. Altitude two, over the real Service and a real memory store, in internal/application/claimable_test.go: for every status that can be SEEDED, a real Claim of a real prepared Increment, asserting SUCCESS for each of the four admitting statuses -- which is how non_goals item 3 is measured rather than promised, because it proves claiming still issues the lease, the execution, the fencing token, the event and the outbox item unchanged -- and asserting REFUSAL for each of the seven others, with needs-input refused by ErrAwaitingHumanInput and the other six by ErrRequirementNotClaimable. One cell is measured to need care: seeding `completed` requires a StableSnapshot, because internal/domain/model.go:324-328 makes a completed Requirement without ReleaseID, BundleDigest and EvidenceDigest fail Validate, and internal/application/human_input_test.go:52-75's seedRequirementStatus calls domain.Validate before saving. Build that snapshot by concatenation and record it; if a cell cannot be seeded at all, record it with its measured reason and never as a pass.
decisions.rationale: Non_goals item 3 -- do not change what claiming does when the state admits it -- is the one that a partial test set cannot defend, because the natural test to write is 'the refusal happens' and that test is compatible with a claim that now fails in some admitting state nobody sampled. Asserting all four admitting statuses succeed, at the altitude where the lease and the execution are real, is the only form that closes it. Splitting into two altitudes is the honest accounting: the predicate can be proved over all eleven statuses for free, while the Service-level table can only reach the statuses the store can be seeded into, and the completed cell's Validate dependency is the concrete illustration of why the second list is shorter than the first.

decisions.decision: Every migrated fixture must NAME the status it establishes, at its seeding site, as a domain constant literal -- and the mechanism is capped at one helper per package. The in-tree idiom already exists and is already parameterised by the target status: internal/application/human_input_test.go:52 declares seedRequirementStatus(t, st, id, status) which reads the Requirement, sets the status, increments the Version, calls domain.Validate and saves, and human_input_test.go:107's buildHumanInputFixture takes the desired status as its third argument and is called as buildHumanInputFixture(t, "iff-waiting", domain.RequirementActive) at :562. internal/api/api_test.go has the same idiom twice, seedActiveRequirement at :2382-2384 and pinMakeActive at :3670, the latter carrying the comment 'no /v1 route advances it'. Measured, that is also why internal/api/api_test.go's pin table needs NO migration: pinMakeActive already puts pin-loop into `active`, so pin row 'claim-accepted' at api_test.go:4047 still returns 200 with the guard in place. This task adds AT MOST ONE such helper per affected package -- internal/reconciler, internal/runner and internal/store/firestore have none today -- and every call site names the status as a constant, never a variable and never a string.
decisions.rationale: This is the mechanism that makes weakening detectable at review time instead of at incident time. A fixture made green by widening the guard leaves no trace at the fixture; a fixture made green by naming domain.RequirementReady at its seeding site leaves a literal a reviewer reads in one second and a scanner counts mechanically. Capping the helpers at one per package matters for the same reason: three helpers in one package is three places where the next fixture can be seeded to something nobody cross-checked, and the cap makes the total number of places where a Requirement status is set by fiat a small measured integer -- see d11.

decisions.decision: The counting tripwires, all four measured at 9bf0d8c so the after-value is comparable. (i) `grep -rn 'Status = domain.Requirement' --include='*_test.go' .` returns exactly FOUR lines today, all in internal/api/api_test.go -- three RequirementActive and one RequirementFraming. Every increase is a fixture seeded by fiat and must be one row of the migration table; a row naming a status outside the four is the defect. (ii) Per-file claim call-site counts must not DECREASE: `grep -c '\.Claim(\|\.ClaimIncrement(' <file>` over the 18 files that call it returns 46 in total (service_test.go 15, provider_live_test.go 8, human_input_test.go 3, publication_test.go 3, fencing_journey_test.go 2, stop_journey_test.go 2, stop_matrix_test.go 2, and 1 each in allocation_test.go, provider_registry_test.go, repository_test.go, runner_version_test.go, control_agent_test.go, crash_test.go, forgepublish_test.go, journey_test.go, lease_test.go, secret_broker_test.go and internal/store/firestore/store_test.go), and `grep -c 'claims:acquire'` returns 10 in internal/api/api_test.go, 9 in internal/api/live_dogfood_test.go and 1 in internal/application/runner_version_test.go. A deleted claim step is the commonest way to make a fixture pass while measuring less. (iii) Top-level test counts per package must not decrease and no test may be renamed: internal/domain 54, internal/application 187, internal/api 63, internal/contracts 33, internal/reconciler 16, internal/runner 118, internal/store/memory 16, internal/store/firestore 36, internal/ci 11. (iv) Non-test Claim callers stay at THREE: internal/api/api.go:1070, internal/runner/orchestrator.go:57 and the internal/application/service.go:1276 alias.
decisions.rationale: Non_goals item 1 -- do not weaken a fixture to avoid the refusal -- is a prohibition on a class of edits, and a prohibition is only enforceable if the class has a measurable signature. Each of these four numbers is a different signature of the same cheat: (i) catches seeding by fiat, (ii) catches deleting the claim, (iii) catches deleting or renaming the test, (iv) catches moving the claim out of the fixture entirely. All four are single greps, all four have a measured before-value, and none of them can be satisfied by an implementer who did the work honestly.

decisions.decision: The migration is NOT a one-line insert: it moves the parent's Version, and that second wave was measured. A seed or a framing pair increments the Requirement's Version, so every downstream ExpectedRequirementVersion in the same fixture goes stale. Measured by execution: inserting a ready-seed before internal/runner/lease_test.go:62's Plan turned the not-claimable refusal into `lease_test.go:94: stale domain version` on all three TestLeaseKeeper tests, and threading the post-seed version into that Plan's ExpectedRequirementVersion turned the package green. The correct repair is to thread the version; the wrong repairs -- dropping ExpectedRequirementVersion, passing zero, or seeding after Plan -- each remove a real assertion. After V2-084 lands there is a THIRD wave: Claim itself issues the ready-to-active transition, so the parent's version moves again at the claim, and any fixture that afterwards issues a Requirement command or asserts a version must thread that too. Every version thread is a row of the migration table.
decisions.rationale: This is the finding that makes the difference between a Work Order that describes the task and one an implementer can execute without inventing policy under pressure. An implementer who hits 'stale domain version' three tests into the migration has a fast wrong answer available -- delete the expected version -- and it looks like tidying rather than weakening, because the error message never mentions a Requirement status. Naming the second and third waves in advance, with the measured error string, is what converts that moment from a judgement call into a lookup.

decisions.decision: internal/runner/orchestrator.go is a PRODUCTION file and it must move, which is the strongest available evidence that the admitting state is reachable rather than seeded. RunFakeJourney (orchestrator.go:35-116) drives Capture, Plan, Prepare and Claim while the parent stays at captured, and TestOrchestratorFakeJourney fails with the guard in place -- measured. It cannot use a test helper, so it must use the product's own commands: it already holds an owner context at orchestrator.go:39, so it gains Service.StartFraming and V2-084's Service.CompleteFraming between the Capture at :41 and the Plan at :45, and threads the resulting version into the Plan's ExpectedRequirementVersion. This is the ONE place in the design where the admitting state is established by the product's own path with no store write, and internal/runner/orchestrator_test.go must assert it: the journey's Requirement is `ready` before the claim and `active` after it. Because it is production code with exactly one caller and that caller is a test (measured: `grep -rn 'RunFakeJourney'` returns three lines, the declaration and orchestrator_test.go:56 and :63), fixing it costs no running behaviour and buys the reachability proof.
decisions.rationale: The deepest form of weakening available in this task is not editing a guard; it is migrating all 62 fixtures with store writes, which makes the suite green while leaving the admitting state unreachable through the product. One production journey that reaches `ready` by issuing the product's own commands is the antidote, and this repository happens to contain exactly one such journey. That it is named RunFakeJourney and its only caller is a test is not a reason to treat it as a fixture: it is the only code in the tree that composes the whole owner-to-runner path, and making it frame the Requirement is what proves the migration target is a state the product produces.

decisions.decision: Three fixture sets cannot be executed here, and each is handled differently and honestly. (i) internal/store/firestore/store_test.go:281's claim is skipped without FIRESTORE_EMULATOR_HOST (store_test.go:43-44) and was measured to FAIL by starting scripts/firestore-emulator.sh for real: it must be migrated and the emulator run is mandatory, because a bare `go test ./internal/store/firestore` prints ok while measuring nothing (gate rule G7). Note it claims from two goroutines (store_test.go:278-284), so it is an existing concurrency fixture: the migration must add no goroutine and must not remove that one. (ii) internal/runner/provider_live_test.go has EIGHT claim call sites (:298, :411, :504, :711, :809, :886, :992, :1074) all fed by ONE Capture at :237, and is skipped without AGENTIC_LOOP_LIVE_PROVIDER=1 (:49-51). No Provider CLI invocation is authorised, so it is migrated at that single seeding site by inspection, compiled by `go vet ./internal/runner` and `gofmt`, and recorded as UNEXECUTED with status skipped -- never as a pass. (iii) internal/api/live_dogfood_test.go's four claim journeys are fed by ONE helper, planAndPrepare at :1268-1270, called at :1296, :1469, :1496 and :1882, from Requirements captured through fx.capture at :1028-1040 and left in captured: it is migrated inside that one helper, additively, with no assertion touched, and likewise recorded as UNEXECUTED. Leaving (ii) or (iii) unmigrated would leave a fixture that relies on claiming not asking, which is exactly what this task exists to remove.
decisions.rationale: The alternative to migrating the unexecutable fixtures is to leave two known-broken live journeys as landmines for whoever next runs the dogfood, and to have this task's own outcome sentence be false for them. The alternative to recording them as unexecuted is to pretend a blind edit was verified. Doing both -- edit, and record the edit as unverified with the measured reason -- is the only combination that is neither negligent nor dishonest, and the single-seeding-site measurement is what makes the blind edits small enough to be safe: one helper each, four and eight claim sites downstream.

decisions.decision: What this task makes true beyond its own sentence, and what it deliberately leaves false. It makes V2-090's pause actually stop new claims: once a Requirement is paused, its Increments become unclaimable, which is precisely definition.md:143's '新しい仕事のclaimを止める' and precisely the propagation V2-090's own scope table said it did not deliver. It also closes V2-084's F1 for the cancelled case: a cancelled Requirement's Increments stop being claimable. What stays false, each recorded as a finding and none of them fixed here: an Increment can still be PLANNED and PREPARED under a Requirement that admits no work, because Service.Plan writes the parent without a domain command and this task refuses only the claim; internal/application/readmodels.go:309-332's nextAction still reports 'run next increment' for a ready Increment whose parent admits nothing (readmodels.go:324-325), so the read model advertises an action the claim now refuses, and readmodels.go is prohibited because that string is a claim about what to do next and V2-090 holds the file; a claim from waiting or recovering succeeds and leaves the parent in waiting or recovering, so the aggregate still contradicts domain-model.md:266's definition of active, because V2-084's parent transition fires only from ready; and a lease already held is not revoked when the parent leaves the admitting set, for the reason d6 gives.
decisions.rationale: A guard that refuses claims is easy to over-claim: it looks like it stops work, and it does not. Enumerating the four residual falsehoods with the measurement that leaves each one open is what keeps the evidence honest and gives the coordinator four issuable follow-ons instead of a vague sense that something is unfinished. The nextAction gap is the one most likely to be 'helpfully' fixed, which is why readmodels.go is prohibited rather than merely unmentioned.

decisions.decision: Chain position, components and the manifest, stated as facts. Components: application, api, runner, reconciler, store-firestore -- FIVE evidence records and exactly five evidence keys, of 23 declared components. contracts/openapi/openapi-v1.yaml is NOT edited and contracts_changed is EMPTY, which is a measurement rather than a preference: contracts/openapi/openapi-v1.yaml:144-149 already declares '409' among claims:acquire's responses, and the new refusal reuses the existing 'conflict' code, so the contracts key does not move, the release BundleDigest does not move, and this task does not enrol in the api-contract chain. NO import edge is created or removed: internal/application's new file uses domain, which ci/components.json already declares among application's dependencies; internal/api's one disjunct uses application, already declared; internal/runner/orchestrator.go calls Service methods and already imports application; internal/reconciler and internal/store/firestore tests use application and domain, both already declared. So ci/components.json and Makefile are prohibited, and a red manifest or dependency-coverage check means the design was departed from. Ordering: AFTER V2-084 (which lands Service.CompleteFraming and the ready and start edges this migration depends on, and holds internal/application/service.go, internal/application/framing_test.go, internal/api/api.go, internal/api/api_test.go) and AFTER V2-090 (which holds internal/api/api.go, internal/api/api_test.go and internal/application/readmodels.go, and whose cancel-Intent-denies-claim test this guard can pre-empt), and BEFORE V2-080 under gate rule G6b: nine of this task's allowed paths are in the 76-path live exercise set.
decisions.rationale: The coordinator needs the conflict set, the edge answer and the gate answers, and here two of them are unusually clean. The contract answer is a measured no rather than a judgement, because the response code the refusal needs is already declared -- which also means the cheapest possible transport change, one disjunct on an existing branch. The edge answer is a measured no in all five components, which is the strongest available evidence that a refusal was added rather than a dependency. The ordering answer is the one that is not clean: this task sits behind both V2-084 and V2-090 on four shared files, and it must not be run concurrently with either.

verification: devbox run --pure -e AGENTIC_LOOP_LIVE_LOCAL=1 -- scripts/firestore-emulator.sh go test -count=1 -v -run TestControlPlanePreviewLocalLive ./internal/api
risks: The single largest risk is adding `captured` -- or anything else -- to requirementStatusAdmitsClaim, which makes all 62 fixtures green with zero fixture edits and looks like a one-word decision. The guard is the domain-equivalence assertion of d8: the predicate must equal {s : domain.DecideRequirement(s, RequirementStart) succeeds} union {RequirementActive} over the complete go/ast-derived status axis, and internal/domain/** is prohibited, so admitting captured would require widening internal/domain/model.go:486 in a file this task may not open. A predicate that disagrees with that equivalence is a stop-and-escalate, never a switch case to add.

The second-wave breakage does not mention a Requirement status and therefore does not look like this task's problem. Measured: inserting a ready-seed before internal/runner/lease_test.go:62 produced `lease_test.go:94: stale domain version` on three tests, and the only correct repair is to thread the post-seed version into ExpectedRequirementVersion. Dropping the expected version, passing zero, or moving the seed after Plan each delete a real assertion, and each will look like tidying at the time.

Migrating all 62 fixtures with store writes would leave the suite green while the admitting state is unreachable through the product's own commands. internal/runner/orchestrator.go's RunFakeJourney is the antidote and it is production code: it must reach `ready` through Service.StartFraming and Service.CompleteFraming, and internal/runner/orchestrator_test.go must assert `ready` before the claim and `active` after. The count of `Status = domain.Requirement` writes in test files is FOUR today, all in internal/api/api_test.go, and every increase must be one justified row of the migration table.

Leaving the new refusal unclassified at the transport is measured to produce HTTP 500 internal_error (internal/api/api_test.go:1176 with the guard in place and internal/api/api.go unedited) and to fire V2-088's operator record for an unclassified error. One disjunct on the existing 409-conflict branch at internal/api/api.go:1253-1259 is the whole fix; a new status code, a new error code or a new openapi response would move the contracts key for no reason, since openapi-v1.yaml:149 already declares 409 for claims:acquire.

Widening the shared helper requirementAwaitsHumanInput instead of adding a second one would silently change Service.Renew (internal/application/service.go:284-288), killing renewal for work already in flight -- a harder stop than docs/product/definition.md:143 describes -- and would force the wrong answer on the unknown-parent case, because the two questions have opposite correct answers there. internal/application/human_input.go and human_input_test.go are prohibited so the mistake cannot be papered over, and internal/application/human_input_test.go:534's biconditional will fail loudly if the new refusal leaks into a needs-input fixture or is ordered ahead of the old guard.

internal/application/stop_matrix_test.go's TestStopModeByKindMatrix fails with the guard in place (measured) and its constants are cited by name in docs/product/definition.md:156-159: wantStopMatrixCells is 56 at stop_matrix_test.go:20 and wantStopModeAllowedTotal is 12 at :63. The fixture must be migrated so the matrix measures the permit again; neither constant may move, and a moved constant is a stop-and-escalate.

Three fixture sets are invisible to a plain `go test ./...`: internal/store/firestore/store_test.go:281 (skipped without the emulator, measured to FAIL with it -- gate rule G7), internal/runner/provider_live_test.go's eight claim sites (live-provider gate, and no Provider CLI invocation is authorised) and internal/api/live_dogfood_test.go's four (live dogfood). Migrating only the red tests leaves all three broken, and each must be migrated at its single measured seeding site and recorded as unexecuted with status skipped.

internal/api/api.go, internal/api/api_test.go, internal/application/service.go and internal/application/framing_test.go are held by V2-084, and internal/api/api.go, internal/api/api_test.go and internal/application/readmodels.go by V2-090. Running this task concurrently with either conflicts, and running it BEFORE V2-084 leaves the migration with no Service.CompleteFraming and therefore no way to reach `ready` through the product's own path. V2-084's own A6 measurement -- a claim under a captured parent recorded as succeeding -- has its polarity inverted by this task, and if V2-084 left it as an executable measurement it must be rewritten to assert the refusal.

The migration adds one to three extra mutations per fixture, and internal/quota/quota.go:62's MutationUsage reserves {Reads: 32, Writes: 16} BEFORE the callback can stage anything, while quota.DefaultBudget is {Reads: 25000, Writes: 10000, Deletes: 10000} at quota.go:46 and ReadTransactionUsage is {Reads: 6001, Writes: 1} at quota.go:56. V2-087's in-memory true-up landed at internal/store/memory/store.go:353, so V2-084's four-read-transactions-per-day wall is stale; re-measure both rather than trusting either, advance the injected clock between reads if a budget binds, and do not weaken an assertion or raise a budget.
